strengths: Clear identification and empirical demonstration of a genuine failure mode: dense attention models catastrophically fail when sparsified to dilated patterns (Table 1-2), providing strong motivation

Thorough and convincing experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: training-from-scratch analysis, inference-time sparsification, commonsense reasoning, long-context tasks, retrieval-heavy benchmarks, and scaling studies (200M-2.6B parameters)
Practical value through train-once-adapt-many paradigm: single dense pretraining enabling flexible sparse inference with only 1B token adaptation across multiple dilation sizes
Substantial efficiency gains: 60×+ throughput improvements at D=64 on full models with positive scaling trends at larger scales

Comprehensive technical execution including detailed efficiency measurements (operator/block/end-to-end latency), solid ablation studies (Table 7), and good reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters
Generalizability across sparse patterns: approach works effectively with dilated attention, dilated+local windows, top-k block attention, and layer/head-wise hybrids
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: RAT+ is an incremental modification of RAT with engineering solutions (overlapped chunks, active recurrence learning, joint training) rather than conceptual advances; core recurrence mechanism not novel

Insufficient theoretical justification for key design choices: choice of L*=64 is empirical without principled analysis; resolution adaptation phenomenon (rapid convergence in first 500M tokens) observed but not explained; lazy recurrence learning identified but root causes not explored
Non-negligible accuracy trade-offs at scale: 2-3 point drops at D=64 on commonsense reasoning, larger gaps on some LongBench tasks; while better than complete failure, gaps are meaningful

Incomplete hybrid sparse design exploration: paper acknowledges optimal layer/head-wise configurations are unknown and task-dependent, demonstrating only feasibility rather than systematic optimization
Parameter overhead of extra recurrence projection not fully quantified; paper defers parameter efficiency improvements to future work

Limited scope of comparisons: few comparisons to alternative efficiency approaches (e.g., continued pretraining on mixed patterns), evaluation primarily on English, no comparison to recent efficient methods at comparable scale
Missing theoretical analysis of why dense attention fundamentally cannot adapt to dilated patterns beyond connectivity arguments; would strengthen motivation and generalization claims

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real gap: dense models fail to sparsify into dilated patterns despite their theoretical appeal. The paper clearly demonstrates this failure and proposes a practical solution.

Thorough technical analysis with sound methodology: Section 3 convincingly shows recurrence establishes complete receptive fields; Figure 9 identifies distribution shift issues; joint training strategy is well-justified by the need for explicit recurrence learning incentives.

Comprehensive experimental validation across scales (1.5B-7.6B parameters) and diverse tasks (commonsense reasoning, LongBench, RULER) with detailed ablations (Tables 11-13) justifying all design choices.

Substantial practical efficiency gains: 40-60× throughput improvements at D=64 with only 1-3 point accuracy drops, demonstrating strong efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs on both short and long-context tasks.
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, architecture specifications, comprehensive efficiency benchmarking (Tables 22-25), and promised code release enable community adoption.

Valuable insights: Analysis of why simple sparsification fails and the receptive field argument (Section 3) provides guidance for other sparsification approaches; secondary finding that recurrence improves top-k block attention broadens impact.
weaknesses: Adaptation requirement significantly limits the claimed 'train once, infer flexibly' paradigm: Requires ~1B tokens per sparsification pattern (convergence shown at ~500M tokens in Fig. 8), which is substantial compute cost (~10% of pretraining). The paper acknowledges but doesn't fully address why adaptation is necessary—Section 3's attribution to 'the attention mechanism itself' leaves the phenomenon somewhat unexplained.

Incremental architectural novelty: Recurrence mechanism and overlapped chunking directly borrowed from RAT; full-sequence recurrence is straightforward; joint training on two objectives is a simple strategy. Main contribution is empirical finding that this combination enables flexible inference, lacking strong theoretical novelty.

Design choices primarily empirically driven without principled justification: L*=64 chosen empirically (Figure 7) without rigorous theoretical analysis. Why 64 is optimal for all scales (1.5B-7.6B) remains unclear. Adaptation dynamics remain largely observational—understanding what exactly is being 'adapted' would strengthen claims substantially.

Parameter and implementation overhead not fully characterized: Additional recurrence projection increases parameters beyond standard attention; paper defers parameter reduction to future work. Implementation complexity (FlexAttention, associative scan, online softmax) may limit reproducibility and practical deployment despite promised code release.

Incomplete analysis of secondary contributions: Why recurrence improves top-k block attention (Section 5.2) is interesting but underdeveloped. Head hit-rate analysis (Table 9) is preliminary without mechanistic understanding. This feels somewhat orthogonal to the main narrative, suggesting the core contribution could be sharpened.

Scalability questions remain unresolved: Tested only up to 7.6B parameters while modern models are 70B+. Will 1B-token adaptation remain reasonable at larger scales? Does L*=64 remain optimal for very large models? Environmental cost of per-pattern adaptation not explicitly discussed.

strengths: Well-motivated analysis showing why recurrence is needed for dilated attention (Section 3), with clear evidence from training-from-scratch and inference-time sparsification perspectives
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple scales (1.5B, 2.6B, 7.6B), diverse benchmarks (commonsense reasoning, LongBench, NIAH/RULER), and thorough ablation studies
Solid efficiency gains demonstrating 40-60× throughput improvements at D=64 with reasonable accuracy loss (1-2 points at 7.6B scale)
Demonstrates broader applicability by improving top-k block attention on NIAH retrieval tasks, showing recurrence benefits beyond dilated patterns
Honest discussion of limitations including parameter overhead, adaptation requirements, and unresolved open questions about generalization
Clear presentation with detailed implementation details and reproducible hyperparameters
weaknesses: Critical practical limitation: 1B-token adaptation requirement undermines main benefit—unclear if this approach is better than training specialized RAT models from scratch on similar total compute (1.5B+1B vs 2.5B tokens)
Limited core novelty: linear recurrence from RAT + standard joint training + engineering simplifications; no fundamentally new techniques or insights

Modest prefilling speedups (5-6× at D=16) relative to added complexity, while prefilling is the actual bottleneck in long-context LLM inference; decoding gains, though impressive, matter less in many scenarios
Only scaled to 7.6B; scalability to 70B+ models where efficiency is most critical remains undemonstrated

Mismatch between theory and implementation: full-sequence recurrence (L=T) claimed for simplicity, but effective length enforced only to L*=64; no clear evidence that intermediate dilation levels (D=2,4,8,32) learn appropriate lengths through generalization
Evaluation fairness issues: NIAH requires SFT conflating model capability with fine-tuning; LongBench noted as 'prompt-heavy'; comparisons with Mamba2/GatedDeltaNet use different training setups
Parameter overhead from additional recurrence projections not quantified; leaves 'parameter reduction for future work,' making fair per-parameter comparisons impossible
No comparison with simpler baselines (e.g., progressive dilated attention during pretraining) or direct controlled experiment comparing total compute efficiency
Empirical design choices (L*=64) lack principled justification; no guidance for different settings or model scales
Hybrid configuration optimization not provided; paper acknowledges configurations are 'not optimal' and task-dependent, limiting practical applicability

strengths: Clear problem identification: demonstrates that inference-time sparsification of dense models into dilated attention patterns fails (Table 2), establishing genuine motivation
Well-grounded technical design: strong analysis in Section 3 justifying why recurrence is necessary, with clear design rationale for full-sequence recurrence and active recurrence learning
Comprehensive experimental validation: tests across three model scales (1.5B-7.6B), multiple diverse benchmarks (commonsense reasoning, long-context, retrieval), and extensive ablation studies
Strong empirical results: achieves 1-point PPL loss at 7.6B with 64× attention FLOPs and KV cache reduction; demonstrates improved scaling behavior where dense-sparse gap shrinks with model size
Practical utility: flexible inference paradigm (single model supporting D=1-128) is valuable, with detailed efficiency analysis showing 40-60× throughput gains for decoding
Additional contributions: demonstrates recurrence helps beyond dilated attention, improving top-k block attention (Tables 17-18), indicating broader applicability
weaknesses: Adaptation overhead inadequately justified: requires 1B tokens of post-pretraining adaptation (~1% of 100B budget) with unclear necessity; paper acknowledges 'fully addressing this remains important for future work'

Limited technical novelty: full-sequence recurrence is straightforward extension of RAT, active recurrence learning is just joint training with two loss terms; distribution shift handled through workaround rather than principled solution
Gap between theoretical and actual efficiency gains: prefilling achieves 5.5-6× speedup for D=16 versus 16× FLOPs reduction; requires dedicated CUDA kernels for further improvement

Incomplete practical guidance: hybrid configurations acknowledged as 'feasible rather than optimal' with no systematic method to select them; paper notes different tasks favor different patterns but offers no principled selection approach
Limited mechanistic understanding: analysis of why recurrence enables dilated attention is intuitive but not rigorous; claim about 'complete connectivity' lacks formal justification
Restricted evaluation scope: all experiments on decoder-only LLMs; applicability to encoder-decoder models, very long contexts (100K+), or other modalities unexplored
Unanalyzed training overhead: joint training requires two forward passes per batch, but computational cost versus dense baselines not discussed
Parameter increase deferred: additional recurrence projections increase model parameters with 'parameter reduction left for future work'; non-negligible for efficiency-constrained settings
